INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE 1
Amici are law professors whose scholarship and
teaching focus on civil procedure. Amici have devoted
substantial parts of their professional care ers to
studying that subject, including conducting
theoretical and empirical analyses of how different
procedural orderings shape litigation and regulatory
schemes.
This brief reflects the consensus of the amici that
this Court should affirm the Fifth Circuit’s deci sion
and hold that the rule announced in Caterpillar Inc. v.
Lewis, 519 U.S. 61 (1996), does not extend to a
situation in which a jurisdictional error remains
uncured at the time of judgment . Amici are as
follows:2
Professor David Freeman Engstrom is the LSVF
Professor of Law at Stanford Law School.
Professor Stephen B. Burbank is the David Berger
Professor for the Administration of Justice Emeritus
at the University of Pennsylvania Law School.
Professor Maggie Gardner is Professor of Law at
Cornell Law School.
Professor M yriam Gilles is Catharine Waugh
McCullough Professor of Law at Northwestern
Pritzker School of Law.

1 Pursuant to Supreme Court Rule 37.6, counsel for amici
represent that none of the parties or their counsel  made a
monetary contribution intended to fund the preparation or
submission of this brief. Professor Engstrom, as counsel for
amici, was compensated for his work on this submission by Lyons
& Simmons LLP.
2 Amici’s institutional affiliations are included solely for
identification purposes. The views expressed in this brief do not
reflect the views of those institutions.

2
Professor Maria Glover is the Carmack Waterhouse
Professor of Law at the Georgetown University Law
Center.
Professor David Marcus is Professor of Law at
UCLA School of Law.
Professor Diego Zambrano is Professor of Law at
Stanford Law School.
Professor Adam Zimmerman is the Robert Kingsley
Professor of Law at USC Gould School of Law.
SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT
In Caterpillar, this Court held that all’s well that
ends well where a district court’s “initial
misjudgment” about its own jurisdiction is voluntarily
cured by the parties before entry of judgment. This
case is different. Because the district court’s erroneous
jurisdictional ruling remained interlocutory, the
defect persisted through final judgment. Accordingly,
Caterpillar’s narrow and pragmatic exception simply
does not apply. See Caterpillar Inc. v. Lewis, 519 U.S.
61, 76-77 (1996) (“[I]f, at the end of the day and case,
a jurisdictional defect remains uncured, the judgment
must be vacated.”) (emphasis omitted). As this Court’s
more recent decisions underscore, federal courts may
not turn a blind eye to uncured jurisdictional defects
simply to salvage a judgment. When a district court
lacks subject-matter jurisdiction at the time it enters
judgment, the only appropriate remedy is vacatur.
Lacking doctrinal support for their finality -despiteerror approach, Petitioners and their amici fall back
on lurid tales of far-fetched litigation incentives, onesided claims of prejudice, and the usual , longdebunked warnings about a civil justice system run
amok. On each count, Petitioners and their amici are
simply wrong —and their bare assertions do not

3
withstand even basic empirical scrutiny. Getting
these background facts right is particularly important
where, as here, judge-made rules would not only
nullify congressionally conferred procedural rights
but also disregard significant federalism interests and
frustrate states’ considered policy judgments.
ARGUMENT
I. The Fifth Circuit wisely recognized
Caterpillar’s limited reach.
Petitioners and their amici are swimming against a
strong tide. True, in three decisions scattered across
several decades, this Court chipped away at strict
jurisdictional purity and pushed the boundaries of
federal jurisdiction by permitting court-made rules to
reshape, in certain narrow instances, the federal
courts’ diversity jurisdiction. In Caterpillar, this
Court licensed retroactive jurisdiction where the
parties voluntarily cured the defect on their own, in
order to conserve judicial resources. Caterpillar Inc. v.
Lewis, 519 U.S. 61, 75-76 (1996). Some years before,
in Grubbs v. Gen. Elec. Credit Corp., 405 U.S. 699, 700
(1972), the Court also recognized the utility of the
doctrine of waiver in the suspect circumstance where
a party, having chosen not to object to removal, suffers
an adverse judgment at trial and raises the
jurisdictional issue for the first time in a post -
judgment appeal. See Caterpillar, 519 U.S. at 72 -73
(interpreting Grubbs in this light). Finally, in
Newman-Green, Inc. v. Alfonzo-Larrain, 490 U.S. 826,
836-38 (1989)—a case commenced in  federal court
rather than removed, and so outside Congress’s clear
policy choices in 28 U.S.C. §§  1441, 1446 and 1447—
this Court allowed the court of appeals to dismiss a
non-diverse “spoiler” party under Rule 21  where the

4
party was dispensable and no other party would suffer
prejudice. Id. at 836-38.
More recently, however, this Court has wisely
resisted further jurisdictional flexibility in the name
of efficiency. First, in Lexecon Inc. v. Milberg Weiss
Bershad Hynes & Lerach, 523 U.S. 26, 42-43 (1998), a
statutory construction case interpreting 28 U.S.C.
§ 1407’s remand mandate  in multidistrict litigation ,
this Court unanimously distinguished Caterpillar in
rejecting a harmless -error contention . Values of
finality, economy, and efficiency were relevant in
Caterpillar, this Court explained, only because
jurisdiction was satisfied at the time of judgment and
so did not constitute “continuing defiance of the
congressional condition.” Id. at 43. But Congress’s
command, the Court continued, “would lose all
meaning if a party who continuously objected to an
uncorrected categorical violation of the mandate could
obtain no relief at the end of the day.” Id.
This Court’s decision in Grupo Dataflux v. Atlas
Global Group, L.P. , 541 U.S. 567 (2004) , limited
Caterpillar’s reach in even more decisive terms. Id. at
572-73. Writing for the Court, Justice Scalia
addressed whether a subsequent change in a party’s
citizenship could cure a defect in diversity jurisdiction
present when the lawsuit was filed. The Court held
that it could not, reaffirming the longstanding “time -
of-filing” rule —namely, that jurisdiction must exist
based on the facts at the moment the complaint is
filed. The Court reiterated that “‘the jurisdiction of the
court depends upon the state of things at the time of
the action brought.’” Id. at 570  (quoting Mollan v.
Torrance, 22 U.S. ( 9 Wheat. ) 537, 539 (1824) ). In so
doing, this Court emphasized that Caterpillar did not
announce a new approach to jurisdiction —indeed, it

5
“broke no new ground” —but rather carved out a
narrow, preexisting exception to the usual time -offiling rule. Id. at 572.
The Grupo Dataflux  Court took further pains to
reject any suggestion that considerations of finality,
efficiency, or economy were relevant to the “cure of the
jurisdictional defect.” 541 U.S.  at 574  (emphasis
omitted). This was so, the Court explained, because its
analysis in Caterpillar “took as its starting point that
subject-matter jurisdiction had been satisfied” by the
time judgment was entered. Id. (emphasis omitted).
Values of finality, efficiency, and economy, the Court
made clear, might be deployed to overlook violation of
a congressional condition at an earlier stage in the
case, but those court-directed values have no purchase
where the violation continues through to final
judgment. Id. at 571 (noting that dismissal is required
in such a case “regardless of the costs it imposes”).
Thus framed, Grupo Dataflux  limited Caterpillar’s
reach to cases about statutory defects in removal
procedure, under 28 U.S.C. §  1441(a), not
jurisdictional ones, under 28 U.S.C. §  1332. See 16
Moore’s Federal Practice § 107.151[2][f] (3d ed. 2025);
14C Charles Alan Wright & Arthur R. Miller, Federal
Practice and Procedure § 3723 (Rev. 4th ed. 2025).3

3 That distinction is critical to this case because, as
Respondents ably explain (at 20-21), they neither settled nor
abandoned their claims against Whole Foods. See Cohen v.
Beneficial Indus. Loan Corp. , 337 U.S. 541, 546 (1949)
(underscoring that interlocutory orders “are but steps towards
[the] final judgment in which they will merge”); Dupree v.
Younger, 598 U.S. 729, 735 (2023)  (observing that interlocutory
rulings “merge into the final judgment”). And, because Whole
Foods remained in the case at the time the district court entered
judgment, both the Section 1441(a) and the Section 1332
violations persisted at that judgment’s entry.

6
Reaffirming the principle that federal courts
possess only limited jurisdiction , this Court has thus
wisely signaled a retreat from the fragile position in
Caterpillar, Grubbs, and Newman-Green that
jurisdiction can be salvaged, judgments resurrected,
and Congress’s command ignored where necessary to
preserve judicial resources. This Court should not now
reenter the jurisdiction renovation business by
minting a new, Caterpillar-expanding exception to the
statutory requirements of subject-matter jurisdiction.
Doing so would run roughshod over Congress’s clear
command in the removal statutes, which nowhere so
much as hint at support for the extreme jurisdictional
flexibility that Petitioners urge here.
II. Conscientious judging, not strategic
party behavior, is the right metric for
choosing among approaches.
Even if this Court were inclined to ignore Lexecon
and Grupo Dataflux  and let efficiency concerns
override Congress’s jurisdictional  directives—a tall
order—Petitioners and their amici misread the
strategic incentives involved in this case. Indeed, it is
not party incentives that should occupy the Court here
but rather judicial ones.
A vital aim of civil procedure is to temper costly
forms of strategic behavior by the parties. As Roscoe
Pound cautioned many decades ago, civil procedure
should not enact a “sporting theory of justice.” Roscoe
Pound, The Causes of Popular Dissatisfaction with the
Administration of Justice, Address Before the Annual
Convention of the American Bar Association (Aug. 29,
1906), in 14 AM. LAW. 445, 447 (1906); see also Murr v.
Wisconsin, 582 U.S. 383, 402 (2017)  (warning of the
“risk of gamesmanship”); Giles v. Maryland, 386 U.S.
66, 102 (1967) (Fortas, J., concurring) (arguing that a

7
trial is “not a sporting event”) . For this reason, the
Rules Committee and this Court have long tried to
structure procedures to limit delay and curb discovery
abuse, among other costly forms of procedural
maneuvering. See Hickman v. Taylor , 329 U.S. 495,
508 (1947)  (explaining that limitations on discovery
are appropriate to prevent examination “conducted in
bad faith or in such a manner as to annoy, embarrass
or oppress the person subject to the inquiry”);
Chambers v. NASC O, Inc. , 501 U.S. 32,  46 (1991)
(explaining that courts possess inherent powers to
sanction bad -faith tactics, including “delay ing or
disrupting the litigation”) (citation omitted). But in so
doing, courts and rulemakers must be clear -eyed
about what the incentives are and where they point.
Petitioners and their amici fail badly in that regard
by distorting, at nearly every turn, the strategic
incentives at issue in this case. For starters, the core
of the elaborate account imagined by Petitioners ’
amici is fanciful. On their view, the Fifth Circuit’s
jurisdiction-respecting rule will boost a plaintiff’s
incentive to join non -diverse defendants based in the
hope that, should a remand motion be wrongly denied,
the case might proceed in federal court and, in the
event of an unfavorable trial outcome plus an
appellate court’s assignment of erro r, yield vacatur
and retrial in state court. The prospect of vacatur and
remand, they suggest, will induce plaintiffs to overjoin non -diverse defendants at the outset of a case
with that distant end-game in mind. Atl. Legal Found.
Br. 2; Prod. Liab. Advisory Council Br. 4; Nat’l Ass’n
of Mfrs. Br. 5-6. Cf. Petr. Br. 21 ( asserting “mischief”
supposedly caused by the Fifth Circuit’s approach).4

4 Petitioners, for their part, focus on the fact that Respondents
did not file a Rule 54(b) motion for partial final judgment  as to

8
The reality is that plaintiffs in Respondents ’ shoes
already have powerful incentives to structure their
lawsuit to stay in state court. Litigating in state court
offers numerous advantages, including more familiar
procedures, lower litigation costs, a local judge and
jury, the additional settlement leverage that can come
with litigating against multiple defendants
simultaneously, and preempting a defendant’s effort
to point to the “empty chair” of an absent defendant as
the true culprit. Pursuit of these advantages is
thought to be well within a plaintiff’s prerogatives as
the “master of the complaint” under the American way
of law. Royal Canin U.S.A., Inc. v. Wullschleger , 604
U.S. 22, 35 (2025) (“The plaintiff is ‘the master of the
complaint,’ and therefore controls much about her
suit.”) (citation omitted) ; Ala. Great S . Ry. Co. v.
Thompson, 200 U.S. 206, 216 (1906)  (“[T]he plaintiff
may elect his own method of attack.”).5

Whole Foods . But both Petitioners, no less than Respondents,
had the ability , if they were confident in the district court’s
jurisdictional ruling, to seek a Rule 54(b) certification as to Whole
Foods and achieve finality, but they did not do so.
5 It should also be noted that defendants, no less than
plaintiffs, have strong forum preferences—and typically prefer
federal court. See 4 LAWRENCE G. CETRULO, TOXIC TORTS
LITIGATION GUIDE § 47:38 , Westlaw (database updated
Feb. 2025) (“Generally, civil defendants prefer to litigate in
federal court. Reasons cited by defendants as to why they favor
federal jurisdiction include a more favorable appointed judge,
favorable rules of discovery, a potential choice of venue out of the
state, and a more diverse jury pool. Another common
generalization of federal courts is that they are more likely to
dismiss a pleading on a motion to dismiss or summary
judgment.”); see also Neal Miller, An Empirical Study of Forum
Choices in Removal Cases Under Diversity and Federal Question
Jurisdiction, 41 AM. U. L. REV. 369, 392-423 (1992).

9
Given these already-existing incentives, it is highly
unlikely that a rational plaintiff, in framing a lawsuit
at its outset, would be further moved to join a non -
diverse defendant  based on the slim and distant
prospect of a do -over after a twisting chain of events
that includes removal, an erroneous remand ruling,
an adverse trial outcome, and an appellate court’s
determination that the trial court committed error in
denying a remand motion. That convoluted, Palsgrafian sequence is far too speculative and remote to
impact how cases are framed or complaints drafted at
the outset of a case. Indeed, in Caterpillar itself, this
Court rejected a similarly attenuated chain of events
grounded in a dubious assumption regarding
“defendants’ readiness to gamble that any
jurisdictional defect, for example, the absence of
complete diversity, will first escape detection [and ]
then disappear prior to judgment.” Caterpillar, 519
U.S. at 77. The absurdity of the “gamble” imagined by
Petitioners and their amici in this case  is further
underscored by the paucity of cases in which the
court’s subject -matter jurisdiction was called into
question post -judgment—at best, a small handful
every few years. See infra Part III and Appendix A.
In truth, neither side in cases like this one—neither
plaintiffs nor defendants—is likely to craft a filing or
removal strategy at the front -end of a case  based on
the remote chance of vacatur at the case’s distant
back-end. Put more concretely, d efendants are no
more likely to over-remove cases under Petitioners’
finality-despite-error rule than are plaintiffs to overjoin non-diverse defendants under the Fifth Circuit’s
jurisdiction-respecting approach. Because both
parties already face far more potent incentives to steer
the case into one forum or another , this Court should

10
not be distracted by the efforts of Petitioners’ amici to
smoke out perverse incentives that simply do not
exist.
Rather than consider the effect of competing rules
on the parties’ incentives, it would be far more
productive for this Court to instead consider the effect
of those rules on judges. As a respected procedure
scholar has noted, an alternative rule in  Caterpillar
that elevate d jurisdictional boundaries over  finality,
economy, and efficiency would have had a “powerful
effect on federal district judges, encouraging them to
police their removal jurisdiction more carefully rather
than risk an embarrassing and wasteful removal and
appeal.” Amanda L. Tyler, After Justice Ginsburg’s
First Decade: Some Thoughts About Her Contributions
in the Fields of Procedure and Jurisdiction , 90 GEO.
WASH. L. REV. 1572, 1590 (2022).
This is not to suggest that district judges will “balk
at” applying jurisdictional rules with due care —and
this Court has rightly refused to indulge any such
assumption. Caterpillar, 519 U.S. at 77 . But it does
not follow that this Court must blind itself to the likely
incentive effects of its rulings. Well-crafted procedures
can and should create incentives for judges to
carefully resolve threshold matters before investing
time and energy in more resource -intensive stages of
litigation. See Newman-Green, Inc. v. Alfonzo-Larrain
R., 854 F.2d 916, 923 (7th Cir. 1988)  (noting “the
importance of scrupulous adherence to the
jurisdictional limitations of the federal courts”); Coury
v. Prot, 85 F.3d 244, 249 (5th Cir. 1996)  (noting role
for judges as watchdogs to prevent litigants from
“‘playing fast and loose with the judicial machinery ’
and using the federal courts’ limited subject matter
jurisdiction in bad faith”) (citation omitted). Moreover,

11
a modest, stop -and-think incentive to consider the
soundness of a court’s jurisdiction before permitting a
case to go forward  is entirely consonant with the
principle that federal courts should “presume[] that a
cause lies outside [their] limited jurisdiction ,”
Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of Am. , 511 U.S.
375, 377 (1994), and, further, that they should
narrowly construe the removal statutes to avoid
infringing on a state court’s authority to decide a case
within its jurisdiction, Shamrock Oil & Gas Corp. v.
Sheets, 313 U.S. 100, 108-09 (1941).
Far from fueling perverse party incentives, the Fifth
Circuit’s jurisdiction -respecting rule would promote
efficiency over the long -term. By nudging district
courts to proceed cautiously in deciding remand
motions, the threat of vacatur would  induce more
accurate jurisdictional determinations upfront while
aligning judicial incentives with the federal courts’
role as courts of limited jurisdiction. Not only that, but
the Fifth Circuit’s rule would minimize burdensome
litigation seeking new, judge -made excep tions to
Congress’s directives—enhancing long-term efficiency
without ignoring congressional command. See Grupo
Dataflux, 541 U.S. at 580-81.
III. The Fifth Circuit’s approach more fairly
allocates error costs among the parties
and imposes minimal burden on courts.
Another important aim of procedure is to allocate
error costs in the face of inevitable imperfection. Cf.
Santosky v. Kramer, 455 U.S. 745, 755 (1982) (keying
procedural due process analysis to “how the risk of
error should be distributed between the litigants ”).
When mistakes are made , who should shoulder the
burden?

12
Petitioners offer a bracing answer. Their finality -
despite-error rule would have Respondents bear all of
the cost of the district court’s jurisdictional error: first,
a trial in a court, and with a party structure, they did
not choose; second, the expense of two trials rather
than one if they pursue Whole Foods in a separate
state court action; and third, facing down the near -
certain invocation of issue preclusion by Whole Foods
if they do.
The Fifth Circuit’s jurisdiction-respecting approach,
by contrast, would more evenly and equitably
distribute error costs between the parties. For
starters, vacatur would reduce (but not eliminate) the
costs to plaintiffs in Respondents’ shoes —requiring
them to incur the expense of conducting a second trial,
but at least one in the forum they initially chose.
At the same time, vacatur would visit comparably
modest harm on defendants in Petitioners’ position.
True, Petitioners suffered a multi-day trial in federal
court that would be unwound in the event of vacatur,
and they also litigated (but lost) before the Fifth
Circuit in their fruitless effort to defend the district
court’s erroneous jurisdictional ruling. That is an
unfortunate, but hardly unusual, circumstance  in
litigation. See Christianson v. Colt Indus. Operating
Corp., 486 U.S. 800, 818 (1988) (“The age-old rule that
a court may not in any case, even in the interest of
justice, extend its jurisdiction where none exists has
always worked injustice in particular cases. Parties
often spend years litigating claims only to learn that
their efforts and expense were wasted in a court that
lacked jurisdiction.”); see also  Grupo Dataflux , 541
U.S. at 569  (dismissal after three years of pre -trial
litigation and a six -day trial) . But the claims of
Petitioners and their amici are nonetheless

13
exaggerated in this regard. Every good lawyer knows
that pre-trial litigation is where many and even most
litigation costs accrue. JAMES S. KAKALIK ET AL .,
RAND INST. FOR CIVIL JUST., DISCOVERY
MANAGEMENT: FURTHER ANALYSIS OF THE CIVIL
JUSTICE REFORM ACT EVALUATION DATA, at xxi (1998).
So does this Court. See Grupo Dataflux, 541 U.S.  at
577 (noting that pretrial litigation, particularly
discovery and motions practice, often accounts for a
large portion of litigation costs).
Here, those costs are sunk . Much of the pretrial
work performed in the run-up to trial before the
district court would transfer, more or less seamlessly,
to any remanded state court case  against both
defendants. See 8A Charles Alan Wright & Arthur R.
Miller, Federal Practice and Procedure § 2044.1 (3d ed.
2025) (noting that the “prevailing approach” permits
the use of discovery materials obtained in one
proceeding in another action to reduce expense); TEX.
R. CIV. P. 203.6(b) (authorizing use of depositions in
the “same proceeding,” defined to include “a
proceeding in a different court but involving the same
subject matter and the same parties”).
Petitioners’ proposal that plaintiffs should bear  all
of the cost of the district court’s jurisdictional error
rests on their further unfounded assertion (at 29) that
the vacatur required by the Fifth Circuit’s rule would
impose substantial and unnecessary burdens on
federal and state courts. See also Atl. Legal Found. Br.
4-5; Nat’l Ass’n of Mfrs. Br. 6 -20. Their contention s
here are demonstrably false.
To begin, federal courts would incur burdens only if
the Fifth Circuit’s jurisdiction -respecting approach
landed more cases in federal court. But, as just noted
in Part II, plaintiffs are no more likely to over-join

14
defendants under the Fifth Circuit’s rule based on a
distant endgame after a twisting chain of events than
are defendants to over-remove to federal court under
Petitioners’ alternative approach. Much as Petitioners
try to convince the Court otherwise, this is not a case
about perverse party incentives. And, as already noted
in Part II , the Fifth Circuit’s jurisdiction -respecting
rule will lower the burden on federal courts by
creating salutary incentives for district judges to
conscientiously consider their own jurisdiction before
advancing a case.
A more general  problem with the court -burden
claims of Petitioners and their amici is that the
number of cases that might trigger the endgame of
vacatur or retroactive jurisdiction under either
approach is likely to be vanishingly small. Indeed, a
comprehensive search of both reported and
unreported cases in Westlaw turned up only 42 cases
between 1990 and 2025 —slightly over one per year.
See Appendix A. And all but one went up on appeal
from a dispositive motion, not a trial —a finding that
is entirely consistent with the near -complete
vanishing of trials throughout the American legal
system. See generally Nora Freeman Engstrom, The
Diminished Trial, 86 FORDHAM L. REV. 2131 (2018) .
While hard-won experience conducting empirical legal
studies suggests that dozens of hours of further
research using direct PACER docket searches or
similar tools might turn up a handful of  additional
cases, the total is all but certain to remain something
less than a very small blip on the federal court radar.
The remaining empirical assertions by Petitioners’
amici that relate to court burdens—that federal and
state courts are “chronically clogged” (Atl. Legal
Found. Br. 5) and laboring under “crushing” caseloads

15
(Nat’l Ass’n of Mfrs. Br. 3), and that tort claims are on
the rise (Nat’l Ass’n of Mfrs. Br. 17 -18)—do not
survive even basic empirical scrutiny.
Far from “chronically clogged” or laboring under
“crushing” caseloads, federal and state courts have
seen substantial reductions in docket loads in recent
years. Start with federal courts. As reflected in Figure
1 below, federal district court filings declined
precipitously between 2020 and 2024 after a spike in
filings caused by a single multidistrict litigation. Zoom
out and federal civil case filings have hovered around
280,000 per year for twenty years, despite substantial
population growth (roughly 17 percent) over that
same period.6

The empirical claims made by Petitioners’ amici
about tort-filing trends are similarly shoddy. In fact,
federal court tort filings declined nearly 70 percent

18
Drop down to the state level and tort cases have
almost entirely disappeared from court dockets.
Today, torts account for just 4 percent of state -level
case filings, a sharp drop from the mid -1980s, when
personal injury cases made up about 20 percent of
state court civil filings, and the mid-1990s, when such
cases made up roughly 16 percent of filings.  See
Engstrom, Supplying, supra; Joe Palazzolo, We Won’t
See You in Court: The Era of Tort Lawsuits Is Waning,

(reviewing a wide range of empirical research).  The

particularly sharp.  See Myungho Paik et al., The

1—National Trends, 10 J. EMPIRICAL LEGAL STUD.

The reasons for tort’s disappearance from federal
and state court dockets are many. Tort reform efforts
have surely played a role . See generally STEPHEN
DANIELS & JOANNE MARTIN, TORT REFORM,

So has the surge in binding arbitration. See Elizabeth
G. Thornburg, Contracting with Tortfeasors:
Mandatory Arbitration Clauses and Personal Injury
Claims, 67 LAW & CONTEMP. PROBS. 253 (2004) .
Whatever the cause, and as Justice Gorsuch no doubt
knows, the majority of civil cases filed in state courts
are not torts but instead contract actions, primarily
debt collections, evictions, and home foreclosure cases
that pit an institutional plaintiff, typically with a
lawyer, against an individual defendant without one.

In short, clear thinking and rigorous data put the lie
to the assertions of Petitioners  and their amici about
party costs and court burdens. Even if the Court was
inclined to elevate finality, efficiency and economy
over jurisdiction and Congress’s considered policy
judgment, Petitioners’ finality-despite-error approach
heaps all of the error costs on the wrong party. The
Fifth Circuit’s jurisdiction-respecting rule , in

20
IV. The Fifth Circuit’s jurisdictionrespecting rule is more faithful to
federalism values.
Petitioners’ finality-despite-error approach raises a
final and substantial risk of harm: By supercharging
Caterpillar’s emphasis on judicial economy above all
else, Petitioners’ approach would undermine
federalism values by frustrating the considered policy
choices of the many states. In stark contrast, the Fifth
Circuit’s jurisdiction-respecting rule would do no such
injury to state sovereignty interests.
The injury to state sovereignty under Petitioners’
proposed finality -despite-error approach is two -fold.
First, whenever a federal court exercises judicial
power without first establishing its jurisdiction, the
federal court intrudes upon the sovereign ter ritory of
the state in which it sits.  “[O]ur Constitution
establishes a system of dual sovereignty” that divides
power “between the States and the Federal
Government.” Gregory v. Ashcroft , 501 U.S. 452, 457
(1991). Recognizing th at state sovereignty is an
important safeguard of liberty , this Court has long
presumed that Congress legislates with the aim of
“preserv[ing] ‘the constitutional balance between the
National Government and the states.’” Bond v. United
States, 572 U.S. 844, 862 (2014)  (quoting Bond v.
United States , 564 U.S. 211, 222 (2011) ). Indeed, to
displace that presumption, Congress must use
“exceedingly clear language.” U.S. Forest Serv. v.
Cowpasture River Pres. Ass’n , 590 U.S. 604, 62 2
(2020).
This federalism canon takes on special salience
when interpreting statutes that confer jurisdiction.
“Out of respect for state courts, this Court has time
and again declined to construe federal jurisdictional

21
statutes more expansively than their language, most
fairly read, requires.” Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner &
Smith Inc. v. Manning , 578 U.S. 374, 389 (2016); see
also Romero v. Int’l Terminal Operating Co., 358 U.S.
354, 380 (1959)  (“Due regard for the rightful
independence of state governments, which should
actuate federal courts, requires that they scrupulously
confine their own jurisdiction to the precise limits
which the statute has defined.”)  (quoting Healy v.
Ratta, 292 U.S. 263, 270 (1934) ). That interpretive
stance is warranted because whenever a federal court
exercises judicial power without first establishing its
jurisdiction, “ the federal tribunal poaches upon the
territory of a coordinate judicial system, and its
decisions, opinions, and orders are of no effect.”
Howery v. Allstate Ins. Co., 243 F.3d 912, 916 n.6 (5th
Cir. 2001).
The intrusion on sovereignty is particularly sharp
in the case of removal, which wrests from a state court
a legal proceeding that has already commenced, and
does so without any say by the state court. See 28
U.S.C. § 1446(d) (supplying procedures for a “notice of
removal,” not a motion); Shamrock Oil & Gas Corp. v.
Sheets, 313 U.S. 100, 108 -09 (1941) (noting that the
policy underlying removal statutes “is one calling for
the strict construction of such legislation”).
A district court ’s jurisdiction -less exercise of
judicial power also thwarts a state’s control over the
elaboration of its own law. This Court has held that
the “proper construction of state statutes” is “a matter
primarily for determination by the local courts.”
Gilchrist v. Interborough Rapid Transit Co. , 279 U.S.
159, 208 (1929); Harman v. Forssenius, 380 U.S. 528,
535 (1965) (state courts are the ultimate “expositors of
state law”)  (citation omitted) . Federal courts’

22
“pronouncements on the content of state law
inherently involve a significant intrusion on the
prerogative of the state courts to control that
development.” Lexington Ins. Co. v. Rugg & Knopp,
Inc., 165 F.3d 1087, 1092 (7th Cir. 1999)  (citation
omitted).
Even where jurisdiction is proper, a federal court’s
prediction as to  how state  courts would resolve an
issue can burden the states. They often amount to no
more than “ Erie guesses,” as the former Chief Judge
of the Third Circuit has put it. See Dolores K. Sloviter,
A Federal Judge Views Diversity Jurisdiction Through
the Lens of Federalism , 78 VA. L. REV. 1671, 1679
(1992). And federal courts often guess wrong. See id.
at 1677 -78 (cataloging cases); John R. Brown,
Certification–Federalism in Action , 7 CUMB. L. REV.
455, 457 (1977)  (same). These incorrect predictions
“inequitably affect the losing federal litigant ,” sow
confusion, and can even mislead lower courts, who
have “shown a preference for citing federal decisions
on state law instead of state decisions.” See Sloviter,
78 VA. L. REV. at 1681-82.
This case proves the point. The district court went
astray in its fraudulent joinder analysis because it
relied on a series of federal district court decisions
predicting how Texas law would treat claims against
product sellers, instead of focusing on the
authoritative Texas Supreme Court decisions and
Texas state -court opinions interpreting the relevant
statute, as the Fifth Circuit did. See Pet. App. 19a-20a.
By retroactively excusing jurisdictional error,
Petitioners’ approach entrenches Erie guessing and
invites more mispredictions that burden state courts
with potential preclusion tied to non -authoritative
federal readings of state law. By contrast, and as

23
noted in Part II, the Fifth Circuit’s jurisdiction -
respecting rule creates salutary incentives for district
courts to be certain of their jurisdiction before
allowing a case to proceed.
Second, a federal court’s erroneous exercise of
jurisdiction can intrude on state sovereignty by
frustrating the states’ considered policy judgments .
Many states, including Texas, have made a deliberate
policy choice to hold nonmanufacturing sellers liable
in strict product liability actions, whether generally or
in specified circumstances. See Restatement (Third) of
Torts: Product Liability  § 1, cmt. e reporter’s note
(1998) (explaining that “any seller in the chain of
distribution (manufacturer, wholesaler, retailer) is
liable for the sale of a defective product that was a
cause of the plaintiff's injury ” and that “[s] upport for
the rule is widespread”); id. (noting that only a few
“states bar a strict liability action against
nonmanufacturer sellers”) ; Restatement (Second) of
Torts § 402A (1965) (similar); TEX. CIV. PRAC. & REM.
CODE § 82.003(a) (imposing liability on “[a] seller that
did not manufacture a product ” where, inter alia, the
nonmanufacturing defendant made an “express
factual representation about an aspect of the product”
(as was alleged in this case), the nonmanufacturing
defendant “participated in the design of the product,”
the manufacturer is insolvent, or the manufacturer is
not subject to the court’s jurisdiction).9

9 The same is true in admiralty. See, e.g. , THOMAS J.
SCHOENBAUM, ADMIRALTY & MARITIME LAW § 5.13 (6th ed. 2019)
(citing Restatement (Second) of Torts §  402A); Vickers v. Chiles
Drilling Co ., 822 F.2d 535, 538 (5th Cir. 1987)  (applying
Restatement (Second) of Torts §  402A’s liability for “sellers” in
maritime products liability claim).

24
These frameworks reflect a sensible policy
judgment that sellers in the chain of distribution
(including the manufacturer, distributor, wholesaler,
and retailer) should, under at least some
circumstances, be held liable for the sale of a defective
product in order to spread loss and increase the
likelihood of plaintiffs’ recovery.  See, e.g. , Bylsma v.
R.C. Willey, 416 P.3d 595, 606 (Utah 2017) (explaining
that liability for nonmanufacturing sellers  serves the
“policy goal” of ensuring “that the injured plaintiff has
a party from whom she can recover”); Zamora v. Mobil
Corp., 104 Wash. 2d 199, 206 (1985) (noting that “[t]he
primary policy justification” for extending strict
liability to sellers is “provision of the ‘maximum of
protection’ to the consumer”).
Petitioners’ proposed rule would intrude upon these
considered policy judgment s by preventing plaintiffs
in Respondents’ position from pursuing both
manufacturers and sellers in the chain of distribution
in a single action. If adopted, the rule would force
future plaintiffs to bear the cost and burden of filing a
second lawsuit against a wrongly dismissed defendant
while also grappling with preclusion arguments based
on a federal court’s ruling that should never have been
rendered. Some dogged plaintiffs may overcome these
barriers. Many will not.  In either case, by
retroactively excusing a district court’s jurisdictional
error and compelling piecemeal proceedings,
Petitioners’ proposed rule would encumber the state’s
decision regarding how liability is assessed and where
it is assigned. In sharp contrast, the Fifth Circuit’s
jurisdiction-respecting approach , and its vacatur
order in the case below,  ensures that plaintiffs in
Respondents’ position retain the ability to seek full

25
relief against all potentially liable parties in
accordance with state law.
The intrusion on state sovereignty can be no less
acute in cases asserting plain -vanilla (non-product)
negligence claims , especially where states have
adopted several liability . Some states continue to
impose joint-and-several liability on tortfeasors , thus
permitting a plaintiff to recover the full amount of
damages from any culpable defendant, regardless of
that defendant’s share of fault. See, e.g., Holcim (US),
Inc. v. Ohio Cas. Ins. Co. , 38 So. 3d 722 , 729  (Ala.
2009); Shantigar Found. v. Bear Mountain Builders ,
804 N.E.2d 324 , 332  (Mass. 2004) ; VA. CODE ANN.
§ 8.01-443. However, m any ot her states, including
Texas, have abrogated joint -and-several liability by
statute and replaced it with a version of several
liability, which typically requires a court to perform a
comprehensive allocation of damages and fault across
all responsible parties.10
Petitioners’ finality -despite-error approach risks
upending these latter  frameworks. By forcing
plaintiffs to re-file against wrongly dismissed

26
defendants in separate proceedings, Petitioners’
approach invites fragmented litigation  that
undermines the accurate and efficient assignment of
fault among the parties and risks inconsistent
judgments.
In Texas, for instance, a federal court’s allocation of
liability to a wrongly dismissed defendant would enjoy
no preclusive effect in state court . See, e.g., TEX. CIV.
PRAC. & REM. CODE § 33.004(i)(2) ( a finding of fault
against a non-party tortfeasor “may not be used in any
other proceeding, on the basis of res judicata,
collateral estoppel, or any other legal theory, to
impose liability on the person”).  With two courts
independently assigning fault to the defendants, a
plaintiff could be left with a finding of 20 percent
liability as to one defendant and 30 percent as to the
other or, conversely, 70 percent liability as to one
defendant and 80 percent as to the other. The very
real threat of inco nsistent judgments, with some
plaintiffs not made whole and others enjoying a clear
windfall, is a high price to pay to salvage  a federal
district court’s erroneous jurisdictional ruling.
Petitioners’ approach would work an especially
serious intrusion on state sovereignty in jurisdictions
that take the opposite approach—where an allocation
of fault in a single action is treated as the final
adjudication of responsibility for the injury and has
preclusive effect. Indiana provides an illustrative
example. Under the State’s Comparative Fault Act,
the trier of fact must determine “the percentage of
fault of the claimant, of the defendant, and of any
person who is a nonparty.” IND. CODE § 34-51-2-
7(b)(1). The Indiana Supreme Court has explained
that this single action “necessarily adjudicates all the
liability and damages for the plaintiff’s alleged injury”

27
and that issue preclusion bars re -adjudication of this
determination in subsequent litigation against other
tortfeasors. Davidson v. State, 211 N.E.3d 914, 922-23
(Ind. 2023). Under Petitioners’ rule, if a federal court
wrongly retains a diversity case and allocates fault to
the non -diverse party, that allocation will bind the
plaintiff in later state court proceedings —effectively
stripping the state  court of its prerogative to
adjudicate the core state-law question of who is liable
for the injury  sustained by one of the state’s own
citizens.
In short, Petitioners’ proposed approach, by
tolerating a district court’s error and forcing plaintiffs
in Respondents’ shoes to pursue defendants
piecemeal, in multiple courts, will intrude upon state
sovereignty and frustrate the considered policy
judgment of numerous states that several liability is
the best way to achieve an optimal allocation of fault
among responsible parties and an optimal level of care
in protecting the health and safety of their citizens.
CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, t he Court should affirm
the Fifth Circuit’s decision.
